summary: Defines a Telnet option for determining the other module view of the status of options. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Lets one computer ask the other which extra features are switched on right now.

questions: how to query telnet option states
what is the telnet status option
how does telnet status send work
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets one side ask the other what options it currently believes are switched on.

tldr.problem: Telnet peers sometimes need to check what the other end thinks the state of the options is. Simply renegotiating an option could lead to the nonterminating request loop problem described in the Telnet specification.
tldr.mechanism: After the STATUS option (code 5) is agreed with WILL and DO, one side sends IAC SB STATUS SEND IAC SE and the other answers with IAC SB STATUS IS followed by a list of WILL, DO and SB items describing its options.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 651 and lets a user or process verify option states, such as echoing, as the other end sees them.

today: RFC 859 is an Internet Standard and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 651.

sections.title: Command Name and Meanings
sections.content:
The Telnet Status option has the command name STATUS and option code 5. It applies separately to each direction of data flow.

Four commands matter. IAC DON'T STATUS and IAC WON'T STATUS both mean the sender refuses to discuss the current status of options any further. IAC SB STATUS SEND IAC SE asks the receiver to report its own view of the options (SEND is code 1). IAC SB STATUS IS ... IAC SE states the sender's view (IS is code 0). The default is DON'T STATUS and WON'T STATUS, so status is not discussed unless both sides agree.
sections.plainLanguage: There are a few special words: one means "tell me your settings", one means "here are my settings", and two mean "I do not want to talk about settings."

sections.title: Why the Option Exists
sections.content:
The option lets a user or process verify the current state of Telnet options (echoing, for example) as seen by the party at the other end of the connection.

Renegotiating an option to find out its state could lead to the nonterminating request loop problem discussed in the General Consideration section of the Telnet specification. STATUS avoids this by fitting into the normal structure of Telnet options: it defers the actual transfer of status information to the SB subnegotiation command.
sections.plainLanguage: If you keep asking "are you sure?" by flipping the switch again and again, you can get stuck in a loop. Asking for a report is safer.

sections.title: How a Status Exchange Works
sections.content:
WILL and DO are used only to get and grant permission for future discussion. The real status information travels inside subcommands (IAC SB STATUS ...).

Once a WILL and a DO have been exchanged, the sender of the WILL may send status information spontaneously or in response to a request. At worst the information is sent twice. Only the sender of the DO may send requests, and only the sender of the WILL may send actual status information.

Inside an IS report, the items WILL, DO and SB are used exactly as in real option negotiation, except that SB is terminated with SE rather than IAC SE. A data byte SE is sent by doubling it (SE SE). Options not listed are assumed to be in their default states, and a single report describes the condition of all options.
sections.plainLanguage: First both sides agree that a report is allowed. Then the one who agreed to report can send the list, and only the one who asked may ask for it.

sections.title: The Example in the RFC
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, Host1 sends IAC DO STATUS and Host2 replies IAC WILL STATUS. Host2 is now free to send status at any time, and solicitations from Host1 are not necessary.

Host1 may still send IAC SB STATUS SEND IAC SE. Host2 then answers with IAC SB STATUS IS followed by WILL ECHO, DO SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD, WILL STATUS and DO STATUS, ended by IAC SE. The RFC explains this as: Host2 echoes back the data characters it receives, will not send Go-Ahead signals, and will both issue and request status information.
sections.plainLanguage: One computer asks, "Can you tell me your settings?" The other says yes, and then lists them: "I repeat what you type, I do not send go-ahead signals, and I can tell you about settings."
